item.title: How We Legally Defeated Aggressive Anti-Fraud with a Local LLM and Created a Visual-Textual DOM Agent Bypassing Blocks
item.description:
DISCLAIMER: The author strongly condemns malicious use of mass data scraping methods. This article aims to explain how to find necessary information without breaking rules. It details how a common task of finding rare equipment on the secondary market evolved into a full engineering investigation. The author successfully trained a local 7B/8B LLM (Qwen) to bypass aggressive protection systems, obfuscated frontends, and isolated sandbox network restrictions, all without paid search APIs or proxies, using only Python, Playwright, and a pixel-logic approach. The story covers the 'prehistory and pain' of why direct requests to large sites result in bans, and the failure of using search engines as an intermediary. It then introduces the 'Visual Web Agent' method, which involves emulating a real browser and parsing the DOM tree using human-readable markers instead of CSS classes. The steps include using a system Edge browser to avoid headless detection, parsing by text markers to overcome obfuscation, and assembling scattered data using Item IDs. A universal prompt container for the AI agent is provided, followed by the results, highlighting the LLM's autonomy, critical thinking, and the 'proof of concept' that local LLMs can act as autonomous computer operators, seeing the internet like a human user.

item.title: Ru-Jev 1.3: Which unfamiliar category names did the model learn to understand, and which did it not?
item.description:
I have released version 1.3 of Ru-Jev. This is an open model for typed decisions for Russian-language text. It runs on a CPU and can be deployed within a closed loop. In this release, I trained the model to be less dependent on the specific wording used by the caller to name response options. The result is definite. The new version is more accurate than the old one on unfamiliar names that are common or borrowed words. There is no gain on abbreviations and codes. Below, I provide both parts of the result and how I tested them. The model and code are under the MIT license. Weights are available on Hugging Face in the besktech/ru-jev repository. Read more

item.title: Two engineers against deadlines: what two months of agent development taught us
item.description:
In custom development, there are often cases where a project needed to be done yesterday, with tight resources and no available hands. Usually, the choice is limited: either refuse the order or move the deadlines. We became interested in whether it's possible in principle to tackle such an insurmountable task with a limited team by involving AI agents and building a meaningful process around them. We decided to test this in an experiment: the two of us set out to build a complex automation system and set strict time limits. We handed over the coding entirely to the agents, keeping the task definition, control, and testing for ourselves. In two months, we brought the product to the pilot stage and learned firsthand what agent development is truly worth. We want to share this experience. Below is how our process of working with agents is structured, the challenges we faced, and what this experiment taught us. Read on.

item.title: [Translation] Do AI Models Know What They Think? Scientists Are Trying to Find Out
item.description:
What are you thinking about right now? Chances are, you can answer that question without much effort. Awareness of one's own thought processes, a capacity called introspection, or self-observation, seems entirely natural to us. However, among philosophers and psychologists, introspection remains a subject of active debate. Some believe it is closely linked to consciousness. Others argue it is an elaborate illusion. Testing theories of introspection in the lab is difficult, as is defining the phenomenon precisely. Now, after more than a century of studying introspection in humans and animals, researchers are beginning to investigate the phenomenon in new, highly unexpected subjects: large language models. These systems, based on mathematical structures called neural networks, excel at cognitive tasks that only recently seemed exclusively human. But are they also capable of introspection? In 2025, Jack Lindsay, a researcher at Anthropic, developed a way to test introspection in language models by injecting 'thoughts' directly into their neural networks, a kind of targeted digital neurosurgery. Lindsay's experiment showed that the models are at least sometimes capable of detecting and describing such interventions. This closely resembled introspection. Lindsay's paper deliberately confined itself to a narrow set of questions and did not make broader claims about consciousness. (Specifically, it did not suggest that language models have first-person subjective experiences.) Nevertheless, the study sparked a flurry of online reaction. Scientists rushed to replicate Lindsay's experiment on other models. Read more

item.title: Dissecting the Qwen 3.8 27B-1c Brain
item.description:
There is Qwen 3.8 27B, fine-tuned (SFT + LoRA) on a corpus about the 1C:Enterprise platform – the model is available on Hugging Face. The model writes code well in the built-in language, but regularly makes mistakes in the 1C query language: it confuses virtual tables, puts parameters in the wrong place, and mixes in SQL constructs that don't exist in 1C. Attempts to use the classic approach of further fine-tuning the model by collecting new datasets for the 1C query language yield no results. The accuracy gain is less than 1%. And it's a long and painful process. During the struggles with Qwen models and analyzing model usage telemetry, a hypothesis emerged: the model's knowledge of SQL constructs interferes because the lexemes are similar (SELECT, WITH, JOIN, etc.). This leads to the question: can we find specific neurons that "pull" the model towards the wrong answer and carefully suppress only them? The article presents a complete pipeline I've named NERVE (Neuron Editing, Reweighted & Val-Evaluated). Read more

item.title: Is it true that neural networks invent links and why do deleted articles remain in their responses?
item.description:
Under the neural network's response, there is a link, it does not open, and the first thought is that the address is invented. I checked about six hundred addresses from the responses of five neural networks with a search about a month after I collected them. About nine out of ten opened. There are very few dead ones, with 404 and 410 codes. These are addresses of ordinary materials on live platforms, not a random set of characters, so most likely they are deleted articles, not fabrications. It is unknown when exactly they were deleted. Therefore, the risk for the site is different: a link to a deleted page may remain in the sources and lead to emptiness. Read more

item.title: I Spent 200,000 Rubles on Yandex Direct and Realized AI Sales Assistants Should Be Free
item.description:
Everyone who has ever chatted with an online store knows how it ends. You want to ask about one product, and the chat window in the corner first demands your name, phone number, and email. You fill in all three fields, and if it's past ten in the evening, the window promises to reply 'within a minute,' then after a minute it says 'the operator will connect soon,' and then nothing more. By this time, a competitor is already open in a neighboring tab. The store owner has likely already paid for this visit. In a Belarusian plumbing store where my bot currently operates, more than half of those who write in the chat come from paid advertising. I know how much such a visitor costs from my own website: since summer, I've spent about 200,000 rubles on Yandex Direct, and each person who managed to do anything on the site, from clicking a form to registering, cost me over 700 rubles. If such a person closed the window at the phone number field or never got a response, the money for their visit was simply wasted. Read more
